subject: phys
title: P1 – Oscillations and waves
outcomesHtml:
The candidate can:

  1. Analyse oscillation phenomena (trillingsverschijnselen) and represent them graphically: a harmonic oscillation (harmonische trilling) occurs when the resulting force is proportional to and opposite to the displacement, F⃗_res = −C·u⃗; the displacement then follows u(t) = A·sin(2πt/T) with amplitude A and period (periode) T; use f = 1/T, the reduced phase (gereduceerde fase) and the phase difference (faseverschil) Δφ = Δt/T; compute the maximum speed v_max = 2πA/T. (Given u, computing t is not required.)
  2. Make calculations on the natural oscillation (eigentrilling) of a mass–spring system (massa-veersysteem): T = 2π√(m/C) with m in kg and spring constant (veerconstante) C in N/m; know the terms natural frequency (eigenfrequentie) and resonance (resonantie).
  3. Analyse wave phenomena (golfverschijnselen) and represent them graphically, using that sound is a wave phenomenon: running wave (lopende golf), propagation speed (voortplantingssnelheid) v = fλ, echo, speed of sound (geluidssnelheid, in air about 343 m/s at 20 °C, BINAS), speed of light (lichtsnelheid) c = 3.00·10⁸ m/s, transverse (transversaal) and longitudinal (longitudinaal); the phase difference between points Δx apart along a wave is Δφ = Δx/λ.
  4. Determine the physical properties of oscillations and waves from (u,t) and (u,x) diagrams — at least in the contexts cardiogram and oscillogram — and know the links between the amplitude of an oscillogram and the loudness (geluidssterkte) of the tone, and between frequency and pitch (toonhoogte).
  5. For a standing wave (staande golf) analyse the relation between the wavelength and the length of the vibrating medium: node (knoop), antinode (buik), fundamental tone (grondtoon), overtone (boventoon); ℓ = n·½λ (n = 1, 2, …) for a medium fixed or open at both ends, ℓ = (2n − 1)·¼λ for a medium closed at one end; at minimum in the context of musical instruments (muziekinstrumenten).
  6. Explain how the observed wavelength and frequency of a wave change when source and receiver move relative to each other (dopplereffect, new in the 2025 syllabus).
notesHtml:
P1 — Oscillations and waves: notes

English notes on the learning outcomes in README.md. Dutch terms are in brackets and italics. Formula letters follow the CCVX syllabus and BINAS conventions. Built from the CCVX physics syllabus of 15 August 2025.

1. Harmonic oscillation

  • An oscillation (trilling) is a periodic motion around an equilibrium position (evenwichtsstand). The displacement (uitwijking) u is the distance from equilibrium, with a sign (+ above, − below). The amplitude A is the largest displacement.

  • The oscillation is harmonic when the resulting force (resulterende kracht) is proportional to the displacement and points back to equilibrium:

    F⃗_res = −C·u⃗ with C the spring constant (veerconstante) in N/m.

    That single condition (force ∝ −u) is what makes the motion a pure sine: the displacement, speed and acceleration are all sinusoidal in time.

  • Displacement as a function of time: u(t) = A·sin(2πt/T) (when u = 0 and moving up at t = 0; use a cosine or a phase shift otherwise). Exam note from the syllabus: given u you do not have to solve for t.

  • Period and frequency: f = 1/T with T in s and f in Hz.

  • The speed is maximal when passing through equilibrium: v_max = 2πA/T. The speed is zero at the extremes, where the acceleration is maximal.

  • The reduced phase (gereduceerde fase) counts how many whole periods plus a fraction have elapsed. Two identical oscillations shifted by Δt in time have phase difference (faseverschil)

    Δφ = Δt/T (a fraction of a cycle; multiply by 2π for radians or by 360° for degrees).

2. The mass–spring system

  • A mass m (kg) hanging from a spring with spring constant C (N/m) has natural period

    T = 2π√(m/C) and natural frequency (eigenfrequentie) f_eigen = 1/T.

    Note: gravity only shifts the equilibrium position; it does not appear in T. Larger m → slower oscillation; stiffer spring (larger C) → faster.

  • When a system is driven by a periodic force with frequency f_drive ≈ f_eigen, the amplitude grows large: resonance (resonantie). Examples: a child on a swing pushed in the right rhythm, a car body bouncing after a speed bump, rattling at certain engine speeds.

  • The spring constant follows from a static measurement: at rest F_z = C·u, so C = m·g/u with g = 9.81 m/s² (BINAS).

3. Running waves

  • In a running (travelling) wave (lopende golf) the oscillation is passed on through a medium. Each point performs the same oscillation a little later than its neighbour. The wavelength λ is the distance between two points in the same phase (e.g. crest to crest).

  • The propagation speed (voortplantingssnelheid): v = fλ …… a wave covers one wavelength per period, also written v = λ/T.

  • Transverse (transversaal): the oscillation is perpendicular to the propagation (waves on a string, light). Longitudinal (longitudinaal): the oscillation is along the propagation (sound: compressions and rarefactions of air).

  • Sound in air at 20 °C travels at about 343 m/s (BINAS: geluidssnelheid); in water about 1.5·10³ m/s. Light and all electromagnetic waves travel at c = 2.998·10⁸ m/s ≈ 3.00·10⁸ m/s in vacuum (BINAS: lichtsnelheid).

  • Echo: the sound goes out and back, so the distance to the reflector is s = v·t/2 — do not forget the factor 2.

  • Two points Δx apart along the wave train differ in phase by

    Δφ = Δx/λ.

  • Oscillogram readings: a larger amplitude means a louder tone (geluidssterkte); a higher frequency means a higher pitch (toonhoogte).

4. (u,t) and (u,x) diagrams

  • An (u,t) diagram plots the displacement of one point against time: read A and T from it. A cardiogram (ECG) and an oscillogram of a microphone signal are examples.
  • An (u,x) diagram is a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant: read A and λ from it.
  • Combining both gives everything: v = λ/T, f = 1/T, and phase differences from Δt or Δx.
  • Careful with reading: in an (u,t) diagram a "wavelength" has no meaning (the horizontal axis is time), and in an (u,x) diagram the "period" has no meaning.

5. Standing waves

  • A standing wave (staande golf) arises when a wave reflects back and forth in a limited medium and interferes with itself. Fixed points with zero displacement: nodes (knopen); points with maximum displacement: antinodes (buiken). Neighbouring node–antinode distance: ¼λ.
  • The length ℓ of the medium must fit a whole number of half wavelengths:
    • String or pipe open at both ends: ℓ = n·½λ with n = 1, 2, 3, … → λ_n = 2ℓ/n, so the allowed frequencies are f_n = n·v/(2ℓ): a whole series f, 2f, 3f, … (fundamental grondtoon and overtones boventonen).
    • Pipe closed at one end (node at the closed end, antinode at the open end): ℓ = (2n − 1)·¼λ with n = 1, 2, 3, … → only the odd harmonics f, 3f, 5f, …
  • In musical instruments (muziekinstrumenten) the fundamental sets the pitch and the mixture of overtones sets the timbre.

6. The Doppler effect (new in the 2025 syllabus)

  • When source and receiver move towards each other, the observed wavelength is shorter and the observed frequency higher than the emitted one; when they move apart, the observed wavelength is longer and the frequency lower. Classic example: an ambulance siren sounds higher as it approaches and drops in pitch as it passes.
  • Reason (moving source, still air): the source emits f_s wavefronts per second, but while emitting them it moves forward, so the wavefronts ahead of the source are squeezed into a shorter distance. The wavelength ahead becomes λ′ = (v_sound − v_source)/f_s, and the receiver measures a higher frequency f′ = v_sound/λ′ > f_s. Behind the source the wavefronts are stretched: λ″ = (v_sound + v_source)/f_s → f″ < f_s.
  • Reason (moving receiver): a receiver moving towards the source runs into the wavefronts faster, so it counts more fronts per second: higher f′.
  • You must be able to explain the change qualitatively and do simple reasoning with wavefront spacing; the CCVX syllabus lists the Doppler effect with the word "explain" (uitleggen), so a full Doppler formula is not given — but do not be surprised by simple numerical wavefront reasoning as in Example 7 below.

Worked examples

Fully worked examples for the outcomes in README.md. All examples are original.

Example 1 — from numbers to the oscillation

A block on a spring oscillates harmonically with T = 0.80 s and A = 6.0 cm.

a. Give u(t), taking u = 0 at t = 0 (moving upward). b. Compute the maximum speed. c. Compute u at t = 0.10 s.

Solution. a. u(t) = 6.0·sin(2πt/0.80) cm. b. v_max = 2πA/T = 2π·0.060/0.80 = 0.471 m/s ≈ 0.47 m/s. c. u(0.10) = 6.0·sin(2π·0.125) = 6.0·sin(0.785) = 6.0·0.707 = 4.2 cm.

Example 2 — finding the spring constant, then T

A passenger of 60 kg lowers a car's suspension by 1.5 cm when sitting in it. The car body has mass 900 kg.

a. Compute C of the suspension (four wheels together). b. Compute the natural frequency of the car body on its suspension.

Solution. a. At rest F_z = C·u → C = m·g/u = 60·9.81/0.015 = 3.9·10⁴ N/m. b. Oscillating mass ≈ 900 + 60 = 960 kg: T = 2π√(960/3.92·10⁴) = 2π·√0.02447 = 2π·0.1564 = 0.983 s; f_eigen = 1/0.983 ≈ 1.0 Hz. Driving over evenly spaced bumps at about 17 m/s with the bumps 17 m apart would force the car at roughly this frequency → resonance: large, uncomfortable bouncing.

Example 3 — echo depth sounding

A ship sends an ultrasound pulse downward and receives the echo after 0.16 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1.52·10³ m/s (given). How deep is the water?

Solution. The pulse travels down and back: s = v·t is the total path, so depth d = v·t/2 = 1.52·10³·0.16/2 = 1.2·10² m. The factor 2 is the classic error point: 243 m is the full path, not the depth.

Example 4 — reading an oscillogram

An oscillogram of a tuning fork on an oscilloscope shows that 4.0 complete periods take 9.1 ms on the screen. The speed of sound in the room is 343 m/s.

a. Compute the frequency of the fork. b. Compute the wavelength of the sound. c. A second tone sounds louder but equally low. What is the same and what differs in its oscillogram?

Solution. a. T = 9.1 ms/4.0 = 2.275 ms → f = 1/T = 4.4·10² Hz. b. λ = v/f = 343/440 = 0.78 m. c. Same frequency (equal period on the screen) and a larger amplitude (loudness is set by amplitude, pitch by frequency).

Example 5 — organ pipe

An organ pipe open at both ends is 2.72 m long. The speed of sound is 343 m/s.

a. Compute the fundamental frequency. b. Compute the frequency of the first overtone and name it as a harmonic. c. The same pipe with one end closed: fundamental and first overtone?

Solution. a. ℓ = n·½λ with n = 1 → λ = 2ℓ = 5.44 m → f = 343/5.44 = 63.1 ≈ 63 Hz. b. n = 2: λ = ℓ = 2.72 m → f = 126 Hz: the 2nd harmonic, one octave higher. c. Closed pipe: ℓ = (2n−1)·¼λ. Fundamental (n = 1): λ = 4ℓ = 10.9 m → f = 31.5 ≈ 32 Hz. First overtone (n = 2): ℓ = 3λ/4 → λ = 3.63 m → f = 94.6 ≈ 95 Hz — the third harmonic: a stopped pipe has only odd harmonics and sounds an octave lower than the open pipe of the same length.

Example 6 — (u,t) and (u,x) combined

A wave in a rope: the (u,x) snapshot shows crests 1.5 m apart; the (u,t) recording of one point of the rope shows a period of 0.25 s.

a. Compute the propagation speed. b. Compute the phase difference between two points 0.50 m apart. c. Point P is at its maximum at t = 0. At what later times > 0 is P again at maximum, and when is it first in equilibrium?

Solution. a. λ = 1.5 m and T = 0.25 s → v = λ/T = 6.0 m/s (check: v = fλ with f = 4.0 Hz ✓). b. Δφ = Δx/λ = 0.50/1.5 = ⅓ ≈ 0.33. c. Maxima repeat every T: t = 0.25 s, 0.50 s, … First equilibrium after a maximum is ¼ period later: t = 0.0625 ≈ 0.063 s.

Example 7 — Doppler reasoning (new syllabus)

An ambulance drives at 30 m/s towards a standing pedestrian. The siren emits 800 Hz; the speed of sound is 343 m/s.

a. Explain why the pedestrian hears a higher frequency than 800 Hz. b. Estimate the wavelength of the sound ahead of the ambulance and the frequency the pedestrian hears. c. What changes after the ambulance has passed?

Solution. a. While emitting each wavefront, the ambulance keeps driving closer, so the wavefronts ahead of it lie closer together: a shorter wavelength reaches the pedestrian, and because the fronts still arrive at the speed of sound, more fronts arrive per second → higher frequency. b. In one period (1/800 s = 1.25 ms) the sound moves ahead by 343/800 = 0.429 m while the ambulance closes the gap by 30/800 = 0.0375 m, so the spacing of the fronts ahead is λ′ = (343 − 30)/800 = 0.391 m. The pedestrian hears f′ = 343/0.391 = 877 ≈ 8.8·10² Hz — about 77 Hz higher than emitted. c. After passing, the ambulance stretches the wavefronts behind it: λ″ = (343 + 30)/800 = 0.466 m → f″ = 343/0.466 = 736 ≈ 7.4·10² Hz: the pitch drops below the emitted frequency, which is the characteristic "ee-ooh" drop of a passing siren.

questions.questionHtml:
A block hangs from a spring and oscillates harmonically with period T = 0.40 s and amplitude A = 5.0 cm.

a. Compute the frequency. b. Compute the maximum speed of the block.
A mass of 0.250 kg hangs from a spring with spring constant C = 40.0 N/m and oscillates freely. Compute the period of this mass–spring system.

A tuning fork produces the tone a′ with frequency 440 Hz. The speed of sound in the room is 343 m/s.

a. Compute the wavelength of the sound in that room. b. A second fork sounds one octave higher (880 Hz) in the same room. What is its wavelength? Explain.
questions.answerHtml: a. λ = 0.780 m; b. λ = 0.390 m — half as large because f doubled and v is the same
questions.solutionHtml: a. λ = v/f = 343/440 = 0.780 m. b. λ = 343/880 = 0.390 m. The medium is the same, so v is the same; with v = fλ, doubling f halves λ.

questions.questionHtml:
During a thunderstorm you see a lightning flash and hear the thunder 5.0 s later.

a. Compute the distance to the lightning. b. Explain why you may ignore the travel time of the light.
questions.answerHtml: a. s ≈ 1.7 km; b. light covers that distance in microseconds, sound in seconds
questions.solutionHtml: a. s = v_sound·t = 343·5.0 = 1.7·10³ m ≈ 1.7 km. b. The light travels the same distance in t = s/c = 1.7·10³/3.00·10⁸ ≈ 5.7·10⁻⁶ s. Compared with 5.0 s this is utterly negligible, so the 5.0 s delay is essentially all sound travel.

questions.questionHtml:
A cardiogram (ECG) of a resting person shows 5.0 complete heartbeats in 4.0 s.

a. Determine the period and the frequency of the heartbeat. b. Convert this to beats per minute.
questions.answerHtml: a. T = 0.80 s, f = 1.3 Hz (1.25 Hz); b. 75 beats per minute
questions.solutionHtml: a. T = 4.0 s/5.0 = 0.80 s; f = 1/T = 1.25 Hz ≈ 1.3 Hz. b. 1.25 Hz · 60 s = 75 beats per minute.

questions.questionHtml:
A guitar string has a vibrating length ℓ = 65.0 cm and produces its fundamental tone at 110 Hz.

a. Compute the wavelength of the fundamental on the string and the propagation speed of the waves on this string. b. Give the frequency of the first overtone of this string. c. A guitarist presses the string so that the vibrating length halves. What happens to the fundamental frequency and why?
questions.answerHtml: a. λ = 1.30 m, v = 143 m/s; b. f = 220 Hz; c. the frequency doubles to 220 Hz, because f ∝ 1/ℓ at fixed v
questions.solutionHtml: a. Fundamental on a string: ℓ = 1·½λ → λ = 2ℓ = 1.30 m. The propagation speed on the string: v = fλ = 110·1.30 = 143 m/s. b. First overtone is the second harmonic (n = 2): λ = ℓ = 0.650 m → f = 143/0.650 = 220 Hz. c. New length ℓ′ = 32.5 cm, new fundamental λ′ = 0.650 m → f′ = 143/0.650 = 220 Hz. At fixed wave speed on the string, f = v/(2ℓ): halving ℓ doubles f; the tone sounds one octave higher.

questions.questionHtml:
A blow organ has a pipe stopped at one end. The pipe is 42.5 cm long; the speed of sound is 343 m/s.

a. Compute the fundamental frequency of this pipe. b. Compute the frequency of its first overtone and express it as a multiple of the fundamental. c. Why does this pipe have no second harmonic (2 × fundamental)?
questions.answerHtml: a. f₁ ≈ 2.0·10² Hz (202 Hz); b. f ≈ 6.1·10² Hz (605 Hz), exactly 3 × the fundamental (to within rounding) (3rd harmonic); c. in a half-open pipe only odd numbers of quarter wavelengths fit
questions.solutionHtml: a. Stopped pipe: ℓ = (2n − 1)·¼λ. Fundamental (n = 1): λ = 4ℓ = 1.70 m → f = v/λ = 343/1.70 = 202 ≈ 2.0·10² Hz. b. First overtone is n = 2: ℓ = 3·¼λ → λ = 4ℓ/3 = 0.5667 m → f = 343/0.5667 = 605 ≈ 6.1·10² Hz. Ratio: 605/202 = 2.995 ≈ 3 → the third harmonic. c. The boundary conditions (closed end = node, open end = antinode) only allow ℓ = ¼λ, ¾λ, 1¼λ, … — i.e. the odd harmonics. An even number of quarter wavelengths would put a node or antinode at the wrong end, so the second harmonic cannot exist in this pipe.

questions.questionHtml:
Two identical pendulums swing side by side. Pendulum 1 reaches its rightmost position 0.60 s earlier than pendulum 2. The period of each pendulum is 2.4 s.

a. Compute the phase difference between the two pendulums. b. Express the same phase difference in radians and in degrees. c. State what the reduced phase of pendulum 2 is at the moment pendulum 1 has completed exactly 3.0 periods.
questions.solutionHtml: a. Δφ = Δt/T = 0.60/2.4 = 0.25. b. 0.25 · 2π = ½π rad ≈ 1.6 rad; 0.25 · 360° = 90°. c. Pendulum 2 runs 0.25 of a period behind pendulum 1, so its reduced phase is φ₂ = 3.0 − 0.25 = 2.75.

questions.questionHtml:
The displacement of a tuning-fork prong is given by u(t) = 8.0·sin(5.0π·t), with u in centimetres and t in seconds.

a. Give the amplitude, the period and the frequency. b. Compute the maximum speed of the prong. c. Compute the displacement at t = 0.10 s. d. The fork is now struck harder. State what changes in the oscillogram of the recorded sound, and what that means for what you hear (loudness and pitch).
questions.answerHtml: a. A = 8.0 cm, T = 0.40 s, f = 2.5 Hz; b. v_max = 1.3 m/s; c. u = 8.0 cm; d. the amplitude of the oscillogram is larger (the period is the same): the tone is louder but equally high
questions.solutionHtml: a. From u(t) = A·sin(2πt/T): A = 8.0 cm; 2π/T = 5.0π → T = 2π/(5.0π) = 0.40 s; f = 1/T = 2.5 Hz. b. v_max = 2πA/T = 2π·0.080/0.40 = 1.26 ≈ 1.3 m/s. c. u(0.10) = 8.0·sin(5.0π·0.10) = 8.0·sin(½π) = 8.0 cm — the prong is exactly at its largest displacement. (Note: with the syllabus you compute u from t this way; solving t from a given u is not required.) d. Striking harder increases the amplitude of the oscillation and therefore of the oscillogram, while the period (and frequency) stays the same. Larger amplitude in the oscillogram means a louder tone (geluidssterkte); the pitch (toonhoogte), set by the frequency, is unchanged.

questions.questionHtml:
A train approaches a station at 40 m/s while sounding its horn at 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. (NB: the Doppler effect was added to the syllabus in the version of 1 September 2025.)

a. Explain, in terms of the wavefronts the horn emits, why a listener on the platform hears a frequency higher than 500 Hz. b. Estimate the wavelength of the sound ahead of the train and the frequency the listener hears. c. The train passes and moves away at the same speed. Estimate the frequency heard now, and describe the change at the moment of passing.
questions.answerHtml: a. the wavefronts ahead are compressed by the moving source; b. λ′ ≈ 0.61 m, f′ ≈ 5.7·10² Hz; c. f″ ≈ 4.5·10² Hz, a clear drop in pitch at the moment of passing
questions.solutionHtml: a. In each period the horn emits one wavefront, but between two emissions the train itself moves forward. The fronts ahead of the train are therefore squeezed into a shorter distance: a shorter wavelength arrives at the platform. The fronts still propagate at 343 m/s relative to the air, so with v = fλ a shorter λ means a higher observed frequency. b. Per period (T = 1/500 s = 2.0 ms) the sound advances 343·T = 0.686 m and the train closes in by 40·T = 0.080 m, so the spacing ahead is λ′ = (343 − 40)/500 = 0.606 m. The listener hears f′ = 343/0.606 = 5.66·10² ≈ 5.7·10² Hz. c. Behind the train the spacing stretches to λ″ = (343 + 40)/500 = 0.766 m → f″ = 343/0.766 = 4.48·10² ≈ 4.5·10² Hz. At the moment of passing, the observed pitch drops suddenly from about 566 Hz to about 448 Hz — the classic down-jump of a passing horn.

questions.questionHtml:
A child of 22 kg sits on a playground swing. From a static measurement the "spring constant" of the swinging system for small oscillations turns out to be equivalent to C = 3.4·10³ N/m, so the empty seat-plus-child behaves for small amplitudes as a harmonic oscillator.

a. Compute the natural frequency of the loaded swing. b. The child's parent pushes the swing. Explain with the term resonance how small pushes can build up a large amplitude, and state at what frequency the parent should push. c. The child stands up on the seat. The effective oscillating mass becomes 26 kg. Does the natural frequency increase or decrease? Support your answer.
questions.answerHtml: a. T ≈ 0.51 s, f_eigen ≈ 2.0 Hz; b. push in the rhythm of the natural frequency (≈ 2.0 Hz): the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, so the amplitude keeps growing (resonance); c. decrease to ≈ 1.8 Hz
questions.solutionHtml: a. T = 2π√(m/C) = 2π√(22/3.4·10³) = 2π·√0.00647 = 2π·0.0805 = 0.505 ≈ 0.51 s; f_eigen = 1/T = 2.0 Hz. b. If the parent pushes once per period, in the direction of motion, each push adds energy in step with the swing: the driving frequency equals the natural frequency and the amplitude grows — that is resonance. So push with f ≈ f_eigen ≈ 2.0 Hz (once every 0.51 s). c. T = 2π√(m/C): with m larger (26 kg) and C unchanged, T grows, so f decreases: T = 2π√(26/3.4·10³) = 0.549 s → f = 1.8 Hz. The swing oscillates slower.

questions.questionHtml:
A running wave travels along a long cord. In an (u,x) snapshot the crests are 2.0 m apart and the amplitude is 3.0 cm. A video of one point P of the cord gives an (u,t) diagram with a period of 0.50 s.

a. Compute the propagation speed of the wave. b. Compute the maximum speed of point P. c. Point Q lies 1.0 m to the right of P. Compute the phase difference between P and Q and describe their relative motion. d. Another point R lies 0.50 m to the right of P. At the instant P passes through equilibrium going upward, what is the displacement of R (qualitatively)?
questions.answerHtml: a. v = 4.0 m/s; b. v_max = 0.38 m/s; c. Δφ = 0.50: P and Q are in opposite phase — when P is at +A, Q is at −A; d. R is then exactly at an extreme (crest or trough)
questions.solutionHtml: a. From the (u,x) diagram: λ = 2.0 m; from the (u,t) diagram: T = 0.50 s. v = λ/T = 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 m/s (equivalently v = fλ with f = 2.0 Hz). b. v_max = 2πA/T = 2π·0.030/0.50 = 0.377 ≈ 0.38 m/s. c. Δφ = Δx/λ = 1.0/2.0 = 0.50 — a half cycle. P and Q are in counter-phase: displacement and velocity of Q are at each instant exactly opposite to those of P. d. R lies Δφ = 0.50/2.0 = 0.25 (¼ cycle) ahead or behind P (depending on the direction of travel). A point a quarter period removed from a passage through equilibrium is just at a turning point: R is at maximal displacement +A or −A.
